summary: Lunar Lost & Found is a browser game that turns school-age space fans into space detectives. Since the 1960s, NASA has left landers, rovers and tools on the Moon and Mars, but most kids have never heard of them. In our game, players search real orbital photos from NASA's Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) and the HiRISE camera on Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter to find this hardware themselves. Each find unlocks a story card: what the object is, why it was sent and what science it made possible. One example is the laser mirror left by Apollo 11, which still shows us that the Moon moves away from Earth by about 3.8 cm a year. Levels go from easy (the Apollo 11 lander) to expert (finding only rover tracks or parachutes). Hints, zoom and a card album keep kids motivated. The project meets the challenge by linking each piece of discarded equipment to the discovery it made possible. It matters because kids learn by discovery, using the same images real planetary scientists use.
details:
WHAT IT DOES

Lunar Lost & Found is a "Where's Waldo?"-style game played on real NASA orbital images. Players choose a mission (Moon or Mars), zoom into a photo, and click the hardware they find: a lander, a rover or wheel tracks. A correct find unlocks a story card with four parts: what it is, why it went, what we learned, and a close-up photo from the surface. A miss gives a "warmer / colder" hint, then a text clue such as "look for a bright dot with a long shadow".

LEVELS

- Easy (Moon): Apollo 11 lander

- Medium (Moon): Apollo 12 next to Surveyor 3; Apollo 15–17 rovers and wheel tracks

- Hard (Mars): Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, Perseverance, Ingenuity (HiRISE images)

- Expert: find only the traces, such as tracks, parachutes and heat shields

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- Kids learn by discovery, looking at the same images planetary scientists use.

- Every object is linked to a real scientific result, not just a name and a date.

- Kids learn about image resolution in a natural way: a 3 m rover is only a few pixels wide.

- Teachers can use one level as a 15-minute lesson. It is free, runs in the browser and needs no installation.

TOOLS AND TECHNOLOGY

- Static website: HTML, CSS and JavaScript

- OpenSeadragon / Leaflet for zooming into large images

- One objects.json file stores each object: image, position (x, y), hit radius and story text

- Cropped image tiles for fast loading

- Hosting on GitHub Pages, so no server is needed

CREATIVITY

Instead of a list or an encyclopedia, the hardware becomes a hidden object that kids must find themselves. A "close-up vs orbit" comparison shows the same place from the surface and from space. A card album with badges (such as "Lunar Detective") encourages kids to collect every object.

FACTORS WE CONSIDERED

- Age group: short, simple texts for ages 9–14

- Difficulty: a zoomed-in start and step-by-step hints so nobody gets stuck

- Performance: cropped tiles instead of full-size LROC strips

- Credit: every image credited to its source (for example NASA/GSFC/Arizona State University)

- Use of SI: SI tools helped with the slide design, illustrations and text drafting. All SI-generated visuals are clearly labelled. No NASA logos or branding were generated.

NEXT STEPS

A full Mars campaign, a classroom mode with group results, a tablet version, and deep-space objects (Voyager and Pioneer) shown on a route map.
